title: Break-even point
summary: How much you need to sell to cover every cost, and how much to earn what you want.

what: The break-even point is the sales volume at which revenue equals expenses: you neither win nor lose, and you no longer have to keep putting money into the business.
From that point on, every extra dollar of sales contributes to profit. With the same formula you can work out how much to sell to earn what you want.
formula: Tax rate = gross sales ÷ net sales
Variable cost rate = variable costs ÷ net sales
Break-even point = fixed costs ÷ contribution rate
Sales for a profit = (fixed costs + profit before tax) ÷ contribution rate
Gross sales = net sales × tax rate

variables.name: Variable costs
variables.description: Costs that go up and down with sales: raw materials (the cost of goods consumed).

variables.name: Fixed costs
variables.description: Costs that don't depend on sales volume in the short term: staff, rent, utilities, amortization, fees.

variables.name: Contribution rate
variables.description: The share of each dollar of net sales left to pay fixed costs and generate profit.

steps: Work out net sales by subtracting taxes.
Work out the tax rate and the variable cost rate.
Divide the fixed costs by the contribution rate.
For a target profit, add it (before tax) to the fixed costs before dividing.
Multiply by the tax rate to get gross sales.

examples.title: Handbook data
paragraphs: Gross sales $1,118,000 − taxes $332,248.05 = net sales $785,751.95. Tax rate: 1.42.
Break-even point: 313,977 ÷ 0.66 = $475,722.73 of net sales ($478,346.31 with the unrounded rate).

examples.title: Sales to earn what you want
paragraphs: The owner wants $130,000 net a month; before income tax that's 130,000 ÷ 0.65 = $200,000.
With unrounded rates: $783,047.80 net and $1,114,152.43 gross.

notes.text: The handbook adds $130,000 (the net profit) as if it were before tax and gets $672,692 of net sales. That profit still has to pay 35% income tax, so $130,000 falls short: that's why the profit before tax ($200,000) is used here.
The handbook rounds the contribution rate to 0.66 and the tax rate to 1.42. The calculator uses exact values, so results differ slightly.
The contribution margin shows quickly how raising or lowering costs or prices affects results, without rebuilding the whole income statement.

gross-sales.label: Gross sales
gross-sales.placeholder: Sales for the period including taxes (e.g. 1118000)

variable-costs.label: Variable costs
variable-costs.placeholder: Cost of goods consumed in the period (e.g. 270000)

fixed-costs.label: Fixed costs
fixed-costs.placeholder: Salaries, charges, rent, utilities, expenses, amortization and fees (e.g. 313977)

desired-profit-before-tax.label: Desired profit before tax
desired-profit-before-tax.placeholder: Monthly profit you want, before income tax (e.g. 200000)
desired-profit-before-tax.hint: If you think in take-home terms, divide it by (1 − 0.35).

steps.tax-rate: Tax rate = gross sales ÷ net sales = {grossSales} ÷ {netSales} = {taxRate}
steps.variable-cost-rate: Variable cost rate = variable costs ÷ net sales = {variableCosts} ÷ {netSales} = {variableCostRate}
steps.break-even: Break-even point = fixed costs ÷ contribution rate = {fixedCosts} ÷ {contributionRate} = {breakEvenNetSales}
steps.target-sales: Net sales for your profit = (fixed costs + profit before tax) ÷ contribution rate = ({fixedCosts} + {desiredProfitBeforeTax}) ÷ {contributionRate} = {targetNetSales}
steps.target-gross-sales: Gross sales = net sales × tax rate = {targetNetSales} × {taxRate} = {targetGrossSales}
